title: Cell-identity-selective extirpation inside an organ that keeps working

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an intraoperative method that recognizes malignant cells by their biological identity and selectively eliminates them while preserving the functioning tissue around them. Its motivating case is an infiltrative glioma, where malignant cells can intermingle with brain tissue that supports essential functions. The intended advance is to treat the invaded tissue at the level of individual cell identity, extending surgical clearance beyond what can safely be accomplished by removing anatomical volumes. This is a proposed capability, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

Conceptual synthesis: the capability would join recognition, spatially controlled elimination, and functional preservation. Detecting a suspicious cell or region would not suffice; the method would have to eliminate the targeted cells across a defined treatment field without unacceptable injury to neighboring cells, vessels, ducts, or neural circuits. Its surgical identity rests on controlled treatment inside the operative field. Application to the liver or other solid organs is a proposed extension that would require separate demonstration.

significance.text: Conditional assessment: successful cell-selective elimination would expand local treatment where removing more tissue would cause unacceptable functional loss. The immediate achievement would be elimination of targeted malignant cells together with preservation of measured organ function. It could reduce the tradeoff between wider clearance and loss of useful tissue, allowing treatment within an infiltrated region that anatomy-based resection cannot safely remove.

Improved durable local control would be a further, conditional benefit. It would depend on reaching the relevant cells, recognizing heterogeneous malignant identities, eliminating them effectively, and preventing subsequent disease evolution from repopulating the field. Preservation of an early functional measurement would also need to persist: delayed tissue injury could undermine an initially successful procedure. These dependencies separate immediate technical success from lasting clinical benefit.

The scope is local. The capability would not itself treat metastases or other malignant cells outside the treated field, and demonstration in one tumor type and organ would not establish transfer to other cancers or organs. Describing it as deleting a cell identity is a useful analogy for selectivity, but a biological identity is not necessarily a single, stable, exclusive marker. The proposal therefore does not imply a general cure for solid cancer.

missing_breakthrough.text: Proposed engineering requirement: the missing capability is a reliable connection between recognizing malignant identity and selectively eliminating the recognized cells throughout an infiltrated, functioning tissue field. Recognition must distinguish malignant cells from nearby normal and reactive cells well enough to guide treatment. A system that merely makes a region glow, provides a diagnosis from a sampled point, or supports a wider resection would supply only part of this capability.

Scientific and engineering synthesis: identity heterogeneity is a central barrier. A targeting rule would need to cover relevant malignant populations while avoiding normal cells that share some of their molecular features. The elimination mechanism would then need sufficient spatial or biological selectivity to avoid collateral injury, including injury to structures whose disruption can impair function beyond the treated location. Treatment coverage, access to dispersed cells, and the consequences of cell death within intact tissue would all need to be resolved for the particular tumor and organ.

Proposed verification requirement: the system must also connect treatment to credible measurements of residual disease and preserved function. This requires defining the treatment field, determining where treatment actually reached, measuring false-negative detection and incomplete elimination, and monitoring both immediate and delayed injury. No finite combination of imaging and biopsy can establish literal absence of malignant cells everywhere; the practical breakthrough must therefore include a defensible account of detection limits and untreated or unmeasured regions.

current_state.text: The supplied research attributes the clinical background to Elliot and colleagues’ narrative review, published on June 17, 2025. It reports that the review was read only in part during an earlier pass and that the original trial reports were not re-opened. The source index contains the review’s URL and metadata but no retained document or extracted text. Consequently, the following numerical and clinical statements are preserved as attributed reports from that research; the supplied evidence review could not independently verify them.

According to the supplied research’s account of the review, two randomized trials increased complete resection of enhancing high-grade glioma with 5-aminolevulinic acid guidance: from 36% to 65% in Stummer 2006 and from 47.8% to 79% in Picart 2023. The research also reports that the review’s tables showed no statistically significant overall-survival difference in those trials. These figures describe resection outcomes in the stated trial settings, rather than demonstrated elimination of every infiltrative malignant cell. The absence of a statistically significant survival difference would not, by itself, establish equivalence or rule out a survival effect.

The research additionally attributes to the review an introductory range of 15–67% for gross total resection in high-grade glioma. Its relationship to the higher complete-resection rate reported for one trial cannot be resolved from the retained material; populations, definitions, and study settings require inspection before these numbers can be combined. The earlier claim that incomplete resection occurs because function stops the operation is also too categorical: the supplied record does not establish how much of the reported shortfall is caused by functional constraints.

The same research attributes several limitations to visible fluorescence guidance: tumor cells in biopsies from non-fluorescent boundaries, recurrence near the resection cavity despite removal of visible fluorescence, poor negative predictive value, fluorescence in inflamed tissue, and frequent absence of visible fluorescence in low-grade glioma. These reports motivate concern about treating visible fluorescence as a complete map of malignant cells, but their frequency, diagnostic performance, and applicable clinical settings cannot be checked from the supplied excerpts and metadata. Missing retained evidence does not establish that these reports are false.

The research describes quantitative fluorescence and new dyes as being in development, but the supplied record does not establish their performance or developmental stage. It also characterizes point-probe confocal imaging as classifying a contacted spot, without supplying supporting SUR-11 evidence. Those device-specific claims remain unverified here. More broadly, the record establishes neither achievement of the proposed field-clearing capability nor its worldwide absence as of November 1, 2026; no bounded freshness assessment was supplied.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration sequence: establish selective elimination in a large-animal infiltrative-tumor model, followed by evaluation in people whose tumors cannot be cleared by anatomical resection without unacceptable functional loss. Before treatment, specify the malignant identity or identities being targeted, the treatment field, relevant normal tissues, coverage measurements, residual-disease assays, imaging endpoints, functional outcomes, acceptable functional bounds, and follow-up intervals. These are proposed criteria for a convincing demonstration, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Large-animal selective elimination followed by evaluation in eligible people

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clearance assessment: postoperative stereotactic sampling and imaging should find no detectable targeted malignant cells within explicitly stated coverage and sensitivity limits. The evaluation should report where samples were taken, which parts of the field were inaccessible or unsampled, and what burdens of residual disease the assays could miss. Such findings would demonstrate clearance to the tested limits; they would not prove absence throughout the field or literal universality across malignant identities.
completion_criteria.label: No detectable targeted malignant cells within coverage and sensitivity limits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed functional and clinical assessment: prespecified organ-function measures should remain within acceptable bounds immediately after treatment and during follow-up. Local recurrence should be compared with maximal safe resection using a design that addresses baseline differences, preferably randomization where feasible. A matched comparison alone would not remove all confounding. Disease outside the treated field should be reported separately from local clearance, local recurrence, and functional preservation, while remaining part of the overall assessment of patient outcomes.
completion_criteria.label: Acceptable organ function with recurrence compared against maximal safe resection

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: independent teams should reproduce selective elimination and preserved function across a defined range of tumor burdens, identity variation, and anatomical locations. Reports should identify failures, treatment time, achievable coverage, collateral injury, and situations in which recognition or safe elimination breaks down. Success would establish demonstrated breadth within those conditions; extension to another organ, tumor class, or targeting mechanism would require further evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication of selective elimination and preserved function within boundaries

related_concepts.text: SUR-11, Real-time cellular and molecular vision of the intact operative field, is the closest complement. It concerns recognizing and mapping cells or molecular features during an operation; SUR-10 concerns selectively eliminating malignant cells while preserving function. Better vision could support SUR-10, but recognition alone does not demonstrate elimination. Conversely, a biologically selective elimination mechanism might provide some targeting without a comprehensive visual map. The supplied roster establishes this conceptual distinction, not the performance of any particular imaging device.

SUR-06, Autonomous completion of whole operations at expert level, concerns who or what executes an operation. SUR-07, Incisionless resection and reconstruction inside the closed body, concerns access and intervention within the body. Either could eventually incorporate cell-selective treatment, but neither inherently supplies malignant-identity recognition or selective elimination. SUR-10 could also be achieved through a surgeon-controlled procedure using conventional access.

SUR-05, Adult surgical wounds that heal by regeneration rather than fibrosis, addresses tissue repair after injury. SUR-09, Living, perfused autologous replacements for complex parts that grafts do not supply, and SUR-12, Life-sustaining autologous solid organs assembled for implantation, address replacement of damaged or missing tissue. Their potential overlap is preservation or restoration of function. SUR-10 instead seeks to retain the existing organ by eliminating selected cells within it; regenerative healing or replacement would not establish that selective capability.

SUR-01, Operational donor-specific tolerance for the transplants patients actually receive, and SUR-02, Destination-therapy solid-organ xenotransplantation, also involve biological discrimination, but in the context of sustaining transplanted tissue. Their immune and organ-survival goals differ from identifying and eliminating malignant cells in a local operative field. Any shared targeting or immune-control mechanisms would require separate evidence and would not merge the concepts.

unresolved_issues: The review’s full text and original trial reports are needed to verify the exact resection endpoints, percentages, survival analyses, and clinical scope of the reported fluorescence limitations.
The relationship between the reported 15–67% gross-total-resection range and the trial-specific complete-resection rates remains unresolved.
The supplied record does not quantify how functional constraints, visualization limits, tumor anatomy, or other factors contribute to incomplete resection.
No specific targeting identity, elimination mechanism, or solution to malignant heterogeneity is established; the attainable balance of coverage and normal-tissue protection remains open.
The capabilities and developmental stages of quantitative fluorescence, new dyes, and point-probe confocal imaging require supporting evidence.
No freshness assessment establishes whether the exact proposed capability has subsequently been demonstrated; its absence as of November 1, 2026 cannot be concluded from this record.
Appropriate assay sensitivity, sampling coverage, functional bounds, follow-up duration, and reproducibility requirements remain to be selected for a particular tumor, organ, and treatment mechanism.

brief.title: Removing cancer cells while keeping an organ working
possible: A surgeon could recognize and kill cancer cells mixed among healthy brain cells while leaving that part of the brain working. Treatment could reach into invaded tissue that cannot safely be cut away.
why: For people with infiltrative glioma, a brain tumor that spreads among normal cells, this could ease the tradeoff between clearing cancer and preserving brain function. More complete local treatment could also reduce cancer returning near the operation site.

sources.showed: This narrative review examines fluorescent guidance, which makes tissue glow to help surgeons distinguish brain tumors from surrounding tissue.
sources.cited_for: It supports the clinical background on guided tumor removal and the limits of visible fluorescence.
sources.not_established: Guiding tissue removal does not establish selective killing of cancer cells throughout functioning brain tissue.

sources.who: Yung-Ching Chang, Shiuan-Yeh Chen and colleagues
sources.showed: In a preprint, researchers used antibody-coated gold particles that turn light into heat to kill rat brain cancer cells preferentially over normal support cells grown alongside them. Normal cells also died.
sources.quote:
Only CNS -1 treated with b -
Tag@anti-EGFR can cause significant photothermal eradication of GBM cells.
sources.cited_for: The work links biological targeting to preferential cancer-cell killing in mixed cell cultures.
sources.not_established: Cell cultures do not establish complete cancer-cell clearance or preservation of function in an intact organ.

sources.who: Iulia Peciu-Florianu, Nicolas Reyns and colleagues
sources.showed: The Lille team treated 10 patients with light-activated cell killing during surgery, alongside standard care. This small trial had no comparison group and reported no unacceptable or unexpected toxicity.
sources.quote: No unacceptable or unexpected toxicities and no treatment-related deaths occurred during the study.
sources.cited_for: The trial provides early human safety experience with light-activated treatment inside the surgical field.
sources.not_established: The trial does not establish selective clearance, lasting preservation of brain function, or a benefit over standard treatment.

shown: Progress spans preferential cancer-cell killing in laboratory cultures and a small human trial of treatment during brain surgery. These demonstrate parts of the proposed capability, but neither establishes selective clearance throughout invaded tissue while preserving its function.
missing: A targeting rule must recognize varied cancer cells while sparing normal and reactive cells with similar biological features.
Treatment must reach dispersed cancer cells and kill them without unacceptable damage to neighboring cells, blood vessels or nerve circuits.
Clearance measurements must account for missed cells and untreated areas, while follow-up must detect delayed injury and local recurrence.

milestones.label: Selective killing in large animals, then eligible people
milestones.explanation: Selective killing would have to succeed in a large-animal infiltrative tumor model, then be evaluated in people whose tumors cannot safely be cut out. Defined targets, treatment areas and outcomes would make success assessable.

milestones.label: No targeted cancer cells detected within stated limits
milestones.explanation: Precisely located tissue samples and imaging would have to find no targeted cancer cells within stated coverage and detection limits. This would establish measured clearance while accounting for areas and cells the tests could miss.

milestones.label: Preserved function and recurrence compared with safe surgery
milestones.explanation: Organ function would have to remain acceptable over follow-up, with local recurrence compared against the most extensive safe surgery. A fair comparison would establish whether clearance brings lasting benefit without unacceptable harm.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce clearance and preserved function
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce selective killing and preserved function across defined tumor burdens, biological variation and locations. Reporting failures, coverage and injury would establish where treatment works safely.

uncertain: Can any targeting rule cover the relevant cancer-cell populations without harming normal cells that share their features?
What detection limits, sampling coverage, functional thresholds and follow-up duration would make a convincing demonstration?
Would early clearance and preserved function persist despite delayed injury and changes in the surviving cancer?

page.title: Tumor-selective intraoperative ablation of infiltrating glioma
page.definition: During surgery, a treatment would selectively kill glioma cells that have spread among normal cells in brain tissue left in place. The treated tissue would retain its measured function. Japan has approved one related treatment, photodynamic therapy with talaporfin sodium, in which light activates a drug at the surgical site. Establishing clearance requires testing the treated tissue for viable tumor cells and stating both the area sampled and the assay’s detection limit.

goal.need: Glioblastoma cells spread into functioning brain beyond the visible tumor. Even with fluorescence guidance, wider removal can cost patients their independence. After radiotherapy and temozolomide, 55 of 71 patients with evaluable first relapses had regrowth within 2 cm of the original enhancing mass. Killing residual cells where further surgery is unsafe could delay local recurrence while preserving function. Cells beyond the reach of treatment can still grow.

figures.caption: Complete resection of contrast-enhancing tumor in the 2006 ALA-Glioma trial.
figures.note: The full-analysis population contained 270 of 322 randomized patients. Resection was assessed by MRI within 72 hours after surgery.

completion.title: Infiltrating glioma is cleared to assay limits while treated brain retains its measured function.
completion.criterion: A peer-reviewed prospective human study demonstrates that intraoperative treatment eliminates detectable viable glioma cells from a defined region of retained, infiltrated brain. Prespecified tissue assays establish clearance within stated sampling coverage and detection limits; intermixed nonmalignant cells remain viable. Prespecified neurological and local functional tests show no deterioration from baseline at acute and final protocol-defined follow-up. Evidence distinguishes treatment-induced killing from surgical removal. Success applies only to the assessed field and detection limits.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no published joint success test was identified.
completion.basis: Searched EANO surgical guidance, RANO 2.0, PMDA photodynamic-therapy approval material, and INDYGO/DOSINDYGO endpoints for a joint cell-clearance and retained-brain-function test; none was found. EANO sets functional preservation as a surgical goal; Hemerion names eradication with healthy-tissue sparing. MRI response and authorization of photodynamic therapy do not certify clearance of infiltrating cells. The fallback tests bounded cellular clearance and preserved function.

milestones.title: A candidate glioma treatment has antitumor activity and a justified initial human dose.
milestones.criterion: Before first-in-human testing of the pharmaceutical component in advanced cancer, characterize its antitumor activity, mechanism of action and dependence on dosing schedule in target-relevant models. Assess effects on cardiovascular, respiratory and central nervous system function and justify the proposed starting dose from the nonclinical data.
milestones.set_by: International Conference on Harmonisation, ICH S9 sections 2.1–2.4 and 3.1; applicable to the pharmaceutical component in advanced cancer.
milestones.threshold_quote: mechanism(s) of action and schedule dependencies as well as anti-tumor activity of the pharmaceutical should have been made.

milestones.title: At least 6 of 10 patients complete INDYGO treatment without unacceptable or unexpected toxicity.
milestones.criterion: At least 6 of 10 evaluable patients with newly diagnosed glioblastoma complete intraoperative 5-aminolevulinic acid photodynamic therapy after resection, with 200 J/cm² delivered at the balloon surface and no unacceptable or unexpected toxicity during the first four weeks.
milestones.set_by: CHU Lille, INDYGO feasibility target described in the investigators’ published statistical-analysis section; written for newly diagnosed glioblastoma.
milestones.threshold_quote: at least 60% of the enrolled patients (i.e., 6 out of 10)

milestones.title: DOSINDYGO identifies a light dose using its 3+3 escalation and four-week toxicity rule.
milestones.criterion: Assess 400, 600 and 800 J/cm² in successive cohorts, with independent safety review through four weeks ±3 days. A dose-limiting toxicity is an unacceptable and unexpected grade 3 or higher toxicity under NCI-CTCAE v5.0. Escalate if none of three patients has one. If one does, add three at that dose and escalate only if none of the additional three has one. Stop escalation at two limiting toxicities at one dose and enroll three more patients at the preceding dose level. If no limiting toxicity occurs throughout escalation, select the dose with the best progression-free survival within 25 mm of the resection cavity.
milestones.set_by: CHU de Lille, DOSINDYGO protocol 2018_58, EudraCT 2019-004796-40, section E.5.1; written for intraoperative glioblastoma photodynamic therapy.
milestones.threshold_quote: si on observe une TDL chez 2 patients du palier X, alors l’escalade est arrêtée.

milestones.title: Stereotactic photodynamic therapy prolongs progression-free survival in recurrent glioblastoma at α=0.025.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate superiority at one-sided α=0.025 in the Münster trial’s modified intention-to-treat population. Compare biopsy followed by stereotactic 5-aminolevulinic acid photodynamic therapy with biopsy alone, with subsequent care at the investigator’s discretion in both arms. Measure time from randomization to MRI progression under Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology criteria or death from any cause, censoring event-free patients at last follow-up.
milestones.set_by: Universitätsklinikum Münster, protocol UKM12_0017 and its registered final analysis; written for stereotactic photodynamic therapy in recurrent glioblastoma.
milestones.threshold_quote: the one-sided alpha spending function in the two-stage adaptive design was set to 2.5%.

milestones.title: Treatment reduces viable glioma in retained human brain while preserving its measured function.
milestones.criterion: In patients, demonstrate that intraoperative treatment reduces viable infiltrating glioma cells in a defined region of brain left in place and that intermixed nonmalignant cells survive. Prespecified tests of local function and neurological status must show no deterioration from baseline through protocol-defined follow-up. A measured reduction qualifies even if viable glioma cells remain.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback after searching EANO, RANO 2.0 and INDYGO/DOSINDYGO endpoints; no joint cellular-selectivity and local-function criterion was found.

milestones.title: A treatment kills glioma cells at an exposure that spares normal brain cells in a laboratory model.
milestones.criterion: At the same treatment exposure, demonstrate glioma cell death and assess injury to normal brain cells against matched controls. Histology or cell-specific viability measurements must distinguish the tumor response from injury to normal cells and identify an exposure at which the assay detects tumor killing and no treatment-induced injury to the normal cells.
milestones.set_by: Preclinical glioma phototherapy studies comparing tumor killing with normal-brain injury, including the intracranial mouse study of Sandeman et al. and the infiltrated cerebral organoid study of Pedrosa et al.
milestones.threshold_quote: PDT efficacy without causing phototoxic injury to the normal brain tissue.

not_found: No peer-reviewed DOSINDYGO report establishing the recommended light dose was located.
No human report demonstrating cell-resolved clearance of an infiltrated brain field together with preserved local function was located.

results.finding: Rat glioblastoma and astrocyte co-culture, 6 illuminated regions: mean astrocyte death was 33.7% after R-Tag2 photothermal treatment.
results.detail: Anti-EGFR bare tags also produced differential killing in co-culture, with 43% glioblastoma death and 13% astrocyte death at 3 minutes. The experiment with tags alone and no illumination used R-Tag1.
results.quote:
Under 1 min illumination, the average death rate is 33.7% and 58.2% for AS and CNS -1, 
respectively, Fig. 5(A)(C).

results.finding: Rat CNS-1 glioblastoma cultures, sample size unreported for Exp2: mean cell death was about 50% with anti-EGFR bare tags plus laser.
results.quote:
The average cell death rate is around 
~50%, while for CNS-1 treated with b-Tag@IgG and no tags, the average death rate is <2%.

results.finding: Photobac-PDT reduced orthotopic C6 glioma at day 30 without detected normal brain injury in a three-rat experiment.
results.detail: The case label reflects the use of treatment-naive implants. The paper gives the overall experiment size but leaves the number of rats assessed at each histology dose unclear.

results.finding: After Photobac-PDT, 8 of 10 nude mice bearing U87 glioma xenografts were tumor-free at the final assessment.
results.detail: The starting-dose rationale used a tenfold safety factor on rat and dog GLP data, yielding a recommended maximum of 3.3–3.4 mg/m². The case label reflects the treatment-naive efficacy models.
results.quote: Of particular interest is that the PDT efficacy of Photobac methyl ester was demonstrated in nude mice bearing U87 (human glioma) carcinoma, where 8/10 mice were tumor free at day 60 after Photobac injection (i.v.) and exposing the tumor in mice to light.

results.finding: Autopsy series including 1 newly diagnosed glioblastoma patient (3 total) found tissue changes at a mean depth of 12.7 mm after intraoperative PDT.
results.detail: The mean depth describes histopathological changes across the pooled series. The abstract provides no separate depth for the newly diagnosed patient.
results.quote: Microscopic analysis demonstrated histopathological changes reaching depths of 9, 11, and 18 mm (mean: 12.7 mm) from the surface of the cavity of tumor resection, suggesting the therapeutic tissue depth of PDT to be in this range.

results.finding: Autopsy series including 2 recurrent glioblastoma patients (3 total) found tissue changes at a mean depth of 12.7 mm after intraoperative PDT.
results.detail: The mean depth describes histopathological changes across the pooled series. The abstract provides no separate depths for the recurrent patients.
results.quote: Microscopic analysis demonstrated histopathological changes reaching depths of 9, 11, and 18 mm (mean: 12.7 mm) from the surface of the cavity of tumor resection, suggesting the therapeutic tissue depth of PDT to be in this range.

results.finding: In 14 glioma patients treated with intraoperative talaporfin PDT, diffusion MRI changes extended 5–7 mm into the cavity margin without neurologic deterioration.
results.detail: The treated cohort included 11 patients with glioblastoma and 3 with other high-grade gliomas. The source explicitly identifies the controls as newly diagnosed but does not separately state diagnosis versus recurrence status for the treated cohort.
results.quote: In all patients who received photodynamic therapy, linear high signals on DWI in the irradiated area were detected adjacent to the resection cavity and were 5–7 mm in depth from 1 day posttreatment and disappeared in about 30 days without any neurologic deterioration.

results.finding: All 10 of 10 evaluable INDYGO patients completed treatment without unacceptable or unexpected toxicity in the first four weeks.
results.detail: Two of the 12 enrolled patients discontinued before PDT, one because liver dysfunction contraindicated 5-ALA and one because surgery revealed a temporal abscess.
results.quote: No unacceptable or unexpected toxicities and no treatment-related deaths occurred during the study.

results.finding: In 22 patients with recurrent glioblastoma, the one-sided progression-free survival superiority test for stereotactic 5-ALA iPDT gave p = 0.1732.
results.detail: The trial ended before any interim analysis.
results.quote: It could not be demonstrated that the 5-ALA iPDT group differed significantly from the control group in terms of PFS. The observed PFS curves were in favor of 5-ALA iPDT with a hazard ratio of 0.602 (95% CI 0.207, 1.749).

results.finding: Among 10 treated patients with recurrent glioblastoma, the median NIHSS score increased by 1 point from baseline at one month.
In mouse glioma brain slices (n = 4 experiments), Gal-SeNBD-oleamide PDT produced more apoptosis in tumor regions than in nontumor regions (p < 0.0001).
results.detail: The human slice experiment compared treated and untreated tumor tissue. It did not report a normal brain comparator or identify the samples as newly diagnosed.
results.quote:
Notably, we observed
significantly higher levels of NucView Red-stained apoptotic
cells in GFP-positive tumor regions compared to neighboring
GFP-negative non-tumor regions and GFP-negative non-tumor
slices (Figures6dandS17;T a b l eS3).

results.finding: Cultures from 3 patients with recurrent glioma showed cytodestructive changes after chlorine E6 and 25 J/cm² laser irradiation.
results.detail: The discussion cites a separate comparison using HEK293 human embryonic kidney cells. That comparison does not assess injury to normal brain cells.
results.quote:
In the case of recurrent GB cells, the ef-
fective cytodestructive effect  have been achieved  
when LI 25 J/cm 2 applied both in continuous and 
pulse modes.

results.finding: D2C7-IT had a no-observed-adverse-effect level of 0.05 µg in a GLP study of 80 rats supporting a recurrent malignant glioma trial.
results.detail: The paper reports that 40 ng was the lowest dose administered in the recurrent glioblastoma trial. It identifies the rat toxicity thresholds as dosing references and leaves the quantitative link to 40 ng unspecified.
results.quote: Considering the histopathologic and clinical findings, we conclude that the 0.05 µg total dose is the appropriate NOAEL for D2C7-IT in rats.

results.finding: DOSINDYGO reported zero treatment-related serious adverse events at the four-week evaluation of 12 glioblastoma patients.
results.detail: The release gives a pooled safety result. It does not establish the dose-limiting toxicity count at any dose or specify whether the patients were newly diagnosed.
results.quote:
An initial clinical evaluation was carried out 4 weeks after
each treatment: no serious adverse events linked to this new treatment were noted.

results.finding: In one recurrent glioblastoma patient, a cavity-wall lesion removed 5 months after intraoperative photodynamic therapy showed necrosis without evidence of tumor.
results.detail: The later specimen came from a suspected recurrence. The paper provides no pretreatment viable-cell measurement for that site or assay detection limit.
results.quote: The pathological diagnosis was necrotic tissue, and there was no evidence of tumor recurrence

case_label = "Disease setting". Reason: Clinical protocols and outcome series distinguish patients by when in the course of disease they receive treatment.

definition = "During surgery, a treatment would selectively kill glioma cells that have spread among normal cells in brain tissue left in place. The treated tissue would retain its measured function. Japan has approved one related treatment, photodynamic therapy with talaporfin sodium, in which light activates a drug at the surgical site. Establishing clearance requires testing the treated tissue for viable tumor cells and stating both the area sampled and the assay\u2019s detection limit.". Reason: The definition gains a clinical comparator and explains what it means to kill infiltrating cells in place.

goal.need = "Glioblastoma cells spread into functioning brain beyond the visible tumor. Even with fluorescence guidance, wider removal can cost patients their independence. After radiotherapy and temozolomide, 55 of 71 patients with evaluable first relapses had regrowth within 2 cm of the original enhancing mass. Killing residual cells where further surgery is unsafe could delay local recurrence while preserving function. Cells beyond the reach of treatment can still grow.". Reason: The site of first relapse measures the clinical problem more directly than the amount of MRI-visible tumor left immediately after surgery.

add statement by European Innovation Council, GlioLighT grant agreement 101129705, 2023: "to selectively eliminate glioma, including diffuse cells.". Reason: The GlioLighT grant identifies a publicly funded program that explicitly targets diffuse glioma cells.

add statement by National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence, Photodynamic therapy for brain tumours, 2009: "should only be used in the context of randomised controlled trials". Reason: NICE states the evidentiary limits on clinical use of the photodynamic approach.
add case "Newly diagnosed". Reason: INDYGO’s feasibility target applies to patients undergoing surgery for newly diagnosed glioblastoma.
add case "Recurrent". Reason: The Münster trial tests treatment at recurrence, a population for which clinical series also report outcomes separately.

add milestone after None: "A treatment kills glioma cells at an exposure that spares normal brain cells in a laboratory model.". Reason: The existing milestones begin at readiness for human dosing and omit the laboratory comparison of glioma killing with injury to normal brain.

edit m1: criterion = "Before first-in-human testing of the pharmaceutical component in advanced cancer, characterize its antitumor activity, mechanism of action and dependence on dosing schedule in target-relevant models. Assess effects on cardiovascular, respiratory and central nervous system function and justify the proposed starting dose from the nonclinical data."; refs = [8]. Reason: ICH S9 sets a nonclinical drug-development test, while the glioma–astrocyte experiment measures cell selectivity and now has a journal publication.

edit m2: title = "At least 6 of 10 patients complete INDYGO treatment without unacceptable or unexpected toxicity."; criterion = "At least 6 of 10 evaluable patients with newly diagnosed glioblastoma complete intraoperative 5-aminolevulinic acid photodynamic therapy after resection, with 200 J/cm\u00b2 delivered at the balloon surface and no unacceptable or unexpected toxicity during the first four weeks."; threshold_quote = "at least 60% of the enrolled patients (i.e., 6 out of 10)"; threshold_ref = 6; refs = [6]. Reason: The feasibility test needs the patient population and the surface at which light dose is specified, with the observed outcome kept out of the criterion.

edit m3: title = "DOSINDYGO identifies a light dose using its 3+3 escalation and four-week toxicity rule."; criterion = "Assess 400, 600 and 800 J/cm\u00b2 in successive cohorts, with independent safety review through four weeks \u00b13 days. A dose-limiting toxicity is an unacceptable and unexpected grade 3 or higher toxicity under NCI-CTCAE v5.0. Escalate if none of three patients has one. If one does, add three at that dose and escalate only if none of the additional three has one. Stop escalation at two limiting toxicities at one dose and enroll three more patients at the preceding dose level. If no limiting toxicity occurs throughout escalation, select the dose with the best progression-free survival within 25 mm of the resection cavity."; threshold_quote = "si on observe une TDL chez 2 patients du palier X, alors l\u2019escalade est arr\u00eat\u00e9e."; threshold_ref = 7; refs = [7]. Reason: The registered dose rule specifies how to expand or stop a cohort and how to select a dose if no limiting toxicity occurs.

edit m4: title = "Stereotactic photodynamic therapy prolongs progression-free survival in recurrent glioblastoma at \u03b1=0.025."; criterion = "Demonstrate superiority at one-sided \u03b1=0.025 in the M\u00fcnster trial\u2019s modified intention-to-treat population. Compare biopsy followed by stereotactic 5-aminolevulinic acid photodynamic therapy with biopsy alone, with subsequent care at the investigator\u2019s discretion in both arms. Measure time from randomization to MRI progression under Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology criteria or death from any cause, censoring event-free patients at last follow-up."; threshold_quote = "the one-sided alpha spending function in the two-stage adaptive design was set to 2.5%."; threshold_ref = 10; refs = [10]. Reason: The randomized comparison concerns stereotactic treatment after biopsy for recurrent glioblastoma, and the registry result belongs outside its success criterion.

edit m5: title = "Treatment reduces viable glioma in retained human brain while preserving its measured function."; criterion = "In patients, demonstrate that intraoperative treatment reduces viable infiltrating glioma cells in a defined region of brain left in place and that intermixed nonmalignant cells survive. Prespecified tests of local function and neurological status must show no deterioration from baseline through protocol-defined follow-up. A measured reduction qualifies even if viable glioma cells remain.". Reason: The near-completion milestone tests a reduction in viable infiltrating tumor together with preserved function, which the INDYGO questionnaire results do not measure.
